finding: Ability to complete the simulated delivery rose from 49% before training to 82% after, and was 84% at 6 months and 85% at 12 months.
Knowledge declined at 6 and 12 months but stayed above baseline; the authors recommend retraining at least every 12 months.
At 9 months knowledge was back to baseline (72%, p=0.386), while simulated PPH-management skills stayed above baseline (50%, p=0.003); bimanual compression rose from 19% to 48%.
population: Healthcare workers of several cadres, n=89 (Tanzania)

finding: Programme material states skills can deteriorate 50% in the first 3 to 6 months if not practised.
population: Not stated; attributed to an unnamed 2017 RCT

finding: Across general procedural skills, about half of initial gains in accuracy were lost after about 6.5 months without practice; speed held longer (about 13 months). Not measured on propulsion crews.
Same general procedural decay finding applies by analogy only; no study of propellant-loading crews found.
Cognitive and accuracy-based tasks decayed more than physical and speed-based tasks; loss was large after more than a year of non-use.
Discrete procedural skills may show considerable decay within weeks or months of non-use.
Simulator training improved transfer to the live task; instructional strategy mattered more than simulator fidelity. Aviation evidence, used here by extrapolation.
